title: Blakey's encouragement of young composers and nurturing of young musicians
summary: Blakey never dismissed a tune, encouraged everyone to write, and spent his life developing young musicians who then left to lead bands.

bands.name: Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: So let’s talk about Art Blakey and composing. I’m thinking of you taking a tune to Mr. Blakey and why would he like something and not something else?

Well one thing that was unique about Art Blakey, he didn’t dislike anything. He would take any individual’s music and make it work for the ensemble. He might have a suggestion or he might have some constructive criticism, but by and large I never saw Art just dismiss a song. He would find a way to rehearse it, we’d play it a couple of times. Now if he liked it it would get played more maybe than someone else’s compositions, but I never knew Art — because he really encouraged everyone to write music. So in that respect Art was very supportive. Because he knew for the most part most of us were just embryonic with the writing aspect, being young guys, and some of the older musicians were older, maybe 23, 24, they had a little bit more experience with writing or who just had a better ability so that maybe more of their songs would be played. But everyone that came in the band wasn’t Benny Golson or wasn’t, in my time, a Donald Brown or a Mulgrew Miller who wrote really strong compositions. But he found a way to incorporate the music in the Messenger songbook at some point — a Wayne Shorter, or some of these other special artists, but Art really was encouraging. And that’s something that I think sometimes we all talk about the Jazz Messengers, but we all know it’s understated that Art was very, very supportive of young musicians, I mean he made it his whole life’s work to support young musicians as they came up and as they developed. Then they left and he got more young musicians and developed them, and the cycle just continued for I’d say the from the mid-fifties until he passed. So he really did a whole lot in terms of nurturing or creating a foundation for this art form.
Do you know if — a lot of those fellows who started out with him did that training — did most of them leave to become leaders themselves or did he tell them, “Look time for you to move on”?

Well each situation would be different. I think some musicians felt that it was time to leave. I think in some situations he knew when to get another musician out of the nest to say. So every situation was different but we all feel that, at least I can speak for the musicians that I knew, the Freddie Hubbards of the world or the Jackie McLeans or © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

various other artists, that once they left Art there was a certain learning curve that you go through that you did feel a certain comfort level with how to lead bands or you had some experience. Because you got to watch someone in action. And there’s so many things that I — more and more as I become an experienced band leader — I look back to him and say now some of the things that he did make sense, but they didn’t make sense before, or as a young person coming up you didn’t necessarily agree with it but as the leader somebody has to make the decision. And, as President Obama is finding out, people, no matter what the decision is, there’s always going to be someone who doesn’t agree with it and there’s going to be someone who can work with it. But being a leader we have to delegate and not worry about how people feel about you and more so just to be respected for what you are trying to do, and hopefully that’s appreciated.
